Southern Rhodesia, a British colony in southern Africa run by a white minority regime, came before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 1747, adopted on 28 June 1962. The Assembly had weighed the report of its decolonization team. It notes that most people in the colony had rejected the 1961 constitution forced on them.

The text deplores the denial of equal rights and votes to the African majority. It faults Britain for not yet handing all powers to the people of the land, as the 1960 call for an end to colonial rule requires. The fight over Rhodesia would run at the UN for two more decades.
un-ga-res-47:
Thanks close out the story of Resolution 47, passed by the General Assembly on 11 December 1946. A year before, the Assembly had formed a team to drum up support for UNRRA, the relief agency feeding a war-torn Europe, in its final stage. The team now reports back: member states had backed the agency's work to a large degree, and the aid had helped rebuild lands laid waste by war.

The Assembly warmly thanks the team's chair and members for their work. It notes that a small share of the pledged sums had still not come in. The chair is asked to press the states concerned to complete their gifts, so the agency can finish its task in full.
un-ga-res-a-69-47:
Standard arms, the guns and tanks of daily war, do their worst harm close to home. Resolution A/69/47, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, argues that control of such arms must be sought first at the level of regions and sub-regions. Most threats to peace since the Cold War, it notes, flare up between states that share the same corner of the map.

The text recalls a long chain of yearly votes on the point, back to 1993. It holds that keeping a fair balance in the defense strength of states in a region serves calm. Arms control built on local trust, in this view, beats rules imposed from far away.
un-sc-res-47:
Kashmir's fate should rest with its people, holds Security Council Resolution 47, passed on 21 April 1948. India had brought the fight over the state of Jammu and Kashmir to the Council. Both sides had been heard. Peace and order in Kashmir must be restored at speed, the text holds, and both states must do their utmost to halt all fighting.

Both India and Pakistan, the Council notes with pleasure, hold that Kashmir's choice of state should be made by a free and fair vote of its people. The Kashmir team set up in January is grown from three members to five. Its task, to ready and watch such a vote, forms the heart of the text. The vote itself has never been held. The catalog year of 1947 is off by one.

Jizhou Yan, Ya-Xiong Chen, Angela Desmond, and co-authors traced a partnership that controls a blood gene in a 2006 study. Hoxa9 is a gene that helps direct the making of blood cells, and it must be switched on and off at the right times. In hematopoietic cells, the blood-forming cells of the marrow, two regulators share that job.

Cdx4 and Menin co-regulate Hoxa9 expression, each shaping how strongly the gene runs. The pairing matters because Hoxa9 also shows up in leukemia, where blood formation goes wrong. Knowing who controls the gene, and how they cooperate, marks the control points where a treatment might one day intervene.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d47: On October 19, 1943, the day the Moscow Conference opened, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt again. His message is Document 47 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The timing gives the letter its setting even though the record gives it no topic: ministers were meeting in Moscow while the heads of government kept writing over their heads. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series, in the heart of the October papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d147: A second letter from Roosevelt to Ambassador Steinhardt is dated November 20, 1943, and it stands as Document 147 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With the secretary's letter of the same date, the day's Turkish traffic in this volume runs to three items, the heaviest for any embassy that month. The record does not divide their errands. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d247:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 22 November 1943, at eleven in the morning, record a session called mainly to hear the theater envoys. General Marshall opened by inviting Ambassador Winant, back from London, to describe British thinking, with Ambassador Harriman and theater representatives also present.

Winant says the British felt Allied gains in Italy were not being used fast enough, and saw chances to act and to draw Turkey into the war. On Overlord, he reports no wish to drop the operation, but strong resistance to a fixed date, since London feared a signed contract that ignored later changes. The British also wanted Balkan resistance fully used, and in Italy aimed at Rome and its airfields, not the Po valley.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d347:
Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Kirk detailed release instructions for the Cairo communiqué from Tehran on 29 November 1943. The short telegram, approved by President Roosevelt, fixes one of the tightest press timetables of the conference.

Kirk is to give the text to the Office of War Information for publication at half past eleven at night, Greenwich time, on Wednesday 1 December, under a Cairo dateline. News services get the text at five on Tuesday afternoon in Cairo to allow transmission. They get it under strict warning. All of it stays secret until the release hour, with no advance statements or speculation of any kind. Stories must note that all the principals have left Cairo for unannounced destinations, and pictures are released at the same hour. Kirk must also notify the Chinese minister in detail and send the full instructions and text at highest priority to Steve Early in Washington.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d447:
Yet another Combined Chiefs of Staff session fell on December 5, 1943, and its minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, the senior American and British officers who ran the combined war effort, were meeting daily at the Second Cairo Conference. Their task was to settle the strategy that Tehran had only sketched.

The minutes lay out the session in order: attendance, the matters raised, and the decisions the chiefs recorded before passing them to Roosevelt and Churchill. Together with the day's other records, this one helps show a conference working at full speed. It is primary evidence of how the alliance made its hardest military choices.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d547:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant sent a second direct report to President Roosevelt from London on January 14, 1944. Winant's access in Britain, where he was almost a national figure, made his presidential channel unusually rich. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Two Winant reports to the President inside a fortnight show London business pressing on Washington that January. Britain was then straining under six years of war while preparing to host the invasion of France. For readers, Winant's direct reports offer the feel of the allied capital from a man both governments trusted, written while the Tehran and Cairo decisions were being put into practice.
frus-1944-quebec-d47:
Roosevelt wrote again to Churchill on September 1, 1944. It was the second presidential message of the day. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

By September 1944, the two men had corresponded for five years of war. Their habits were set by then. Separate papers covered separate questions, and answers came in kind. Roosevelt's twin messages close the day's work between the capitals. For readers, the pair shows how the allies governed together. They governed at a distance and in writing. Meanwhile, armies moved faster than any conference could follow.
frus-1944-quebec-d147:
Writing from Hyde Park on September 3, 1944, Roosevelt answered Churchill's latest Italian telegram, number 774. He shared the prime minister's confidence that the Allied divisions in Italy were sufficient for the task before them. Their commanders, he trusted, would press the battle unrelentingly to shatter the enemy forces on the Gothic Line.

After that breakthrough, Roosevelt insisted, the divisions must be used where they best aided Eisenhower's decisive drive into Germany. He leaned toward using American forces westward but called himself completely open-minded. The exact employment could be discussed at Octagon. He closed by crediting General Wilson and General Patch impartially for the brilliant success in southern France.
frus-1944-quebec-d247: Hopkins telegraphed Grace Tully, the president's secretary, on September 15, 1944, chasing a decision. He had sent Roosevelt the State Department's September 11 memorandum on the French lend-lease agreement. The Foreign Economic Administration and the State Department were anxious to know whether the president had initialed it. Hopkins asked Tully to help him get an answer the next day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d47: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 8 January 1945, the same day Harriman reported from Moscow. The letter is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Placed side by side, the two messages show the president hearing from his British partner and his Soviet ambassador within a single day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d147:
Mikolajczyk explained his resignation to an American diplomat in London, and the report reached Washington on 25 November 1944. Ambassador Winant's cable passes on Schoenfeld's account of their talk that morning. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol4-1847:

wirnt-wigalois-pfeiffer-1847:
Wirnt von Grafenberg sang of Wigalois, the son of Gawain, in a romance of the early 1200s. Franz Pfeiffer's 1847 edition prints the medieval German poem in full. Wigalois leaves Arthur's court as a young knight with a wheel of fortune for his sign.

His quest takes him against Roaz, a sorcerer whose dark realm has swallowed kings and knights. Monsters, magic, and hard fights line the road as the young hero grows into his name. morte-arthure-alliterative-halliwell-184:
An unknown poet of the north of England told Arthur's last wars in hard, pounding verse. The Alliterative Morte Arthure, in James Halliwell's 1847 edition, prints the Middle English poem complete. Its Arthur is a great king of war, not a dreamer of courts.

Arthur marches on Rome itself, wins an empire in hard fights, then hears that Mordred has seized his throne and queen. He turns home to a last battle that kills him and the flower of his knights. The tale is darker and bloodier than Malory's later telling. The poem ranks among the peaks of medieval English verse.
savage-gorilla-description-1847:
Thomas Savage, a missionary and naturalist on the Gabon coast, named the gorilla to science in 1847. His paper, Notice of the External Characters and Habits of Troglodytes gorilla, gave the beast its first full learned account. The wild man of the woods of sailor tale became, in his hands, an animal of record.

Savage tells the gorilla's size, build, and ways from skins, skulls, and the tales of hunters he trusted. He sets the new ape beside man and the chimpanzee and marks where it stands apart. The paper founded the science of the gorilla at a stroke. All later study of the great ape starts from Savage's page.
twining-memo-1947:
The Air Force's chief of materiel gave the first high word on the flying discs in September 1947. General Nathan Twining's memo of September 23 holds that the thing reported is real and not a dream or fake. His Air Materiel Command had charge of the new reports that summer.

Twining tells of craft that climb and turn past any plane of the age, as pilots had sworn to him. He asks for a full study, and Project Sign was born of that ask. The memo stands at the head of the whole Air Force UFO file. No later paper in the line counts for more.
fbi-roswell-teletype-1947:
Dallas wired Washington the first federal word on Roswell on the night of July 8, 1947. The teletype from Percy Wyly, the FBI chief in Dallas, sends on the Eighth Air Force report of a found disc. The wire went out at 6:17 in the evening, as the tale broke.

Wyly tells that Wright Field has not yet backed the weather balloon line the Army would soon give out. The disc, by the wire, was on its way east for study. The brisk lines catch the case at its first hour, before the cover tale set. The teletype is the Roswell story's first paper trail.
davis-principles-nature-1847:
Andrew Jackson Davis speaks in trance in The Principles of Nature, his vast book of 1847. Davis was a youth from Poughkeepsie with scant school. In trance, he is said to have spoke for hours on God, stars, life, death, and the fate of man. A scribe took down each word. The book is the fruit of those long trance talks.

It came a year ere the Fox raps made his name as a seer of rank. Fans call him the John the Baptist of the new faith. The book is its first great text in his land.
reynolds-wagner-the-wehr-wolf-1847:
George Reynolds sends a cursed man through old Italy in Wagner, the Wehr-Wolf, his serial of 1846 to 1847. Wagner is a sage who sells his soul for youth, wealth, and a dark gift: he turns wolf when the moon is full. Love, crime, and the stake crowd his path through courts, woods, and the grip of the church's sleuths in a rich, wild plot.

The tale ran in cheap parts that crowds bought by the stack. It made the wolf man a star of mass print. Its zest and gore set the tone for cheap horror. It still reads fast.
hopkins-discovery-of-witches-1647:
Matthew Hopkins defends his hunt in The Discovery of Witches, his brief tract of 1647. Hopkins had roamed East Anglia in the war years, paid by towns to find witches. Scores were hanged on his word. Foes in print charged him with fraud and cruel tests: no sleep, bound swims, and pricks for the Devil's mark on the skin of the charged.

His tract replies ask by ask, in a cool, prim tone. He died the same year, young and much cursed. The tract is the chief hunt man's own word. It is a grim self portrait.
boucher-de-perthes-antiquites-celtiques-:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes, a French customs man at Abbeville, brought out the first part of this work in 1847. Its title means Celtic and pre flood finds, in French. For years he had dug worked flints from deep gravel beds by the Somme.

The flints lay with the bones of beasts long dead, such as mammoths and rhinos of the ice age. Boucher de Perthes held that men made those tools in a time far past the flood of the Bible. Mocked at first, he was proved right in 1859, and a new view of man's age was born.
lilly-christian-astrology-1647:
William Lilly was the best known astrologer in England during the Civil War years. His Christian Astrology, printed in 1647, taught the craft in plain English for the first time. It gave working rules that any reader could test at home. The book made Lilly famous across the country.

Three main arts fill the pages. Horary work answers a direct question from a chart cast for the moment it is asked. Election work picks the best time to start a task, and natal work reads a birth chart. Students of the old craft still treat Lilly as their chief guide.
theophilus-essay-upon-various-arts-1847:
Theophilus was a monk and metal hand of the 1100s in Germany. His work, De Diversis Artibus, tells how the arts were then done. Robert Hendrie gave it English dress in 1847 as An Essay Upon Various Arts. The book is the chief text on the craft shops of the mid ages.

Paint, glass, and metal form the three great heads of the work. The monk tells how to grind hues, blow glass, and cast bells and cups. Each step is set down as a hand at the bench would need it. Few books bring the mid age shop so close to life.
bronte-jane-eyre-1847:
Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847, under the name Currer Bell at first. The novel became the defining first-person tale of female independence in Victorian fiction and beyond. Later governess novels and feminist coming-of-age tales all answer to its strong, plain voice here.

Jane, an orphan schooled at harsh Lowood, takes a governess post at Thornfield Hall in Yorkshire. She loves her master Rochester, whose wife, mad and hidden, lives in the attic above. Fire, a torn veil, and a voice on the wind drive the Gothic plot to crisis. Jane flees, inherits money, and returns to wed Rochester on her own free terms at last. Her insistence on equality of soul still gives the love story its sting.
bronte-wuthering-heights-1847:
Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights in 1847, under the name Ellis Bell at first. Many call it the most radical novel of the Victorian era in form and feeling. Its storm-driven metaphysical romance broke every convention of the realist novel of its day completely.

Heathcliff, a foundling from Liverpool, is raised at Wuthering Heights on the Yorkshire moors there. His fierce bond with Catherine Earnshaw survives her marriage to Edgar Linton of the Grange. Her death drives his revenge on both houses across a whole second generation of Earnshaws. Nelly Dean and the baffled Lockwood tell the tale in frames within frames of voice. The moor wind blows through prose unlike any other English novel of its time.
bronte-agnes-grey-1847:
Anne Brontë published Agnes Grey in 1847, under the name Acton Bell at first. The slim novel was her debut, a quiet account of a governess's working life in England. She drew it from her own years in service, which she had found hard and lonely.

Agnes, a parson's daughter, takes posts to help her poor family after her father's losses. Spoiled children and vain parents make her days a test of patience and self-respect in silence. She keeps her faith and her diary, and finds a friend in the curate Weston. A modest inheritance and a small school end her service on her own terms in peace. The book's plain honesty rebukes the glamor that hid governesses' real plight from readers.
dumas-forty-five-guardsmen-1847:
Alexandre Dumas published The Forty-Five Guardsmen in 1847, the conclusion of his Valois trilogy in French. The romance sets Henri III's forty-five Gascon guards against the Guise faction in Paris and Anjou. Critics often call it Dumas at his most cinematic, with duels staged like film scenes.

Chicot returns, older and graver, as the king's realm frays under League and Spanish plots. The forty-five young Gascons, swaggering and loyal, guard a king who trusts almost no one near him. Diana's revenge for Bussy's murder threads through court war and the Salcede trial in Paris. Henri of Navarre waits in the wings as the Valois line nears its bloody end. The trilogy closes with the crown in peril and France on revolution's brink.
emerson-poems-1847:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Poems in 1847, his collected verse of that early period of work. The volume holds Concord Hymn and The Rhodora, the verse counterpart to the famed essays in prose. Emerson's poems favor thought over music, yet several entered the marrow of American memory for good.

Concord Hymn, sung at the battle monument in 1837, gave us the shot heard round the world. The Rhodora finds God and beauty self-sufficing in a wild flower blooming alone in the woods. Hamatreya broods on earth owning men who thought they owned her fields and farms in Massachusetts. Brahma and Days compress his philosophy into quatrains still quoted in schools and speeches across America today. The verse shows the sage in a second, starker dress than the flowing essays.
thackeray-vanity-fair-1847:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Vanity Fair in 1847, a long novel of English society during the Napoleonic Wars. Becky Sharp is a poor, clever orphan set on rising in the world. Her friend Amelia Sedley is kind, gentle, and far less worldly. Their fortunes rise and fall through love, marriage, war, and money troubles.

Thackeray calls his setting a fair where vanity is bought and sold. The Battle of Waterloo changes several lives at the midpoint. No character is a pure hero, as the subtitle warns. Thackeray narrates with wit, pity, and sharp social insight. Vanity Fair stands among the great panoramic novels in English.
prescott-conquest-peru-1847:
William H. Prescott published History of the Conquest of Peru in 1847, a companion to his Mexico volume. Francisco Pizarro and a small band of Spaniards confront the Inca Empire. Atahualpa's capture at Cajamarca, after a massacre in the square, opens the conquest. Civil war among the conquerors follows the empire's fall.

Prescott describes Inca roads, temples, and rule with romantic admiration. Gold, greed, and daring drive his narrative as in the earlier work. He worked, as before, from Spanish chronicles with the help of readers. The two conquest histories made American historiography respected abroad. Peru remains a gripping, if dated, epic of empire's violent birth.
michelet-french-revolution-1847:
Jules Michelet's History of the French Revolution appears in C. Cocks's translation of 1847. Michelet writes the Revolution as France's national epic, with the people as hero. Bastille Day, the festivals, and the great journées glow with patriotic fire. He worked from archives and from the memories of survivors.

Michelet's style is lyrical, swift, and deeply emotional. He loves the Revolution's early hope and grieves its violence. Critics note his bias, yet few deny his power. The history shaped how France remembers 1789 to this day. English readers met romantic history at its height in this version. It remains a moving, partisan classic.
owen-death-of-death-1647:
Owen's Death of Death in the Death of Christ, published in 1647, is the definitive Puritan defense of definite atonement. The question at stake is simple to state: did Christ die for all people, or for the elect in particular? Owen, then a young pastor, argues the second with relentless logic.

He holds that Christ's death actually saves those it was meant for, rather than merely making salvation possible for everyone. His famous trilemma presses opponents to choose what the cross truly achieved. Reformed readers still cite the book as the classic case against universal redemption.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-2-1847:
William Hickling Prescott published Volume 2 of his History of the Conquest of Mexico in 1847, part of his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott, a Boston historian who worked with failing eyesight, drew on Spanish archives and chronicles. Volume 2 carries the story forward from the first volume.

Hernán Cortés and his small force press deeper against the Aztec world, facing alliances, battles, and reverses. Prescott told the tale with a novelist's pace while grounding it in letters and reports of the time. His history set the English-language account of the conquest for generations. This volume keeps the drama of the march and the siege at the center.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-3-1847:
Volume 3 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico appeared in 1847, continuing his four-volume account of the Spanish conquest. Prescott built the work from Spanish documents, soldiers' letters, and Aztec accounts in translation. The story now moves toward its climax in the Aztec capital.

Readers follow Cortés through flight, regrouping, and the long siege of the great lake city. Prescott weighed the cruelty and courage on both sides and described a world being destroyed in detail. His narrative was praised for fairness as well as style. The volume brings the conquest nearly to its end and shows why his history stayed a standard work for so long.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-4-1847:
Volume 4 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico, published in 1847, completes his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott closed the story he had built from archives in Spain and Mexico. The fall of the Aztec Empire and its aftermath fill these pages.

Cortés rules a conquered land, faces rivals and royal inquiries, and ends his career under a cloud. Prescott judged the conquest's violence honestly while admiring the daring of its leaders. He also traced the early years of Spanish rule that followed. With this volume the first great English history of the conquest reached its end, and it shaped views of Mexico for a century.
harvey-motion-of-heart-willis-1847:
William Harvey's On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals appears here in Robert Willis's 1847 Sydenham Society translation. Harvey published De motu cordis in Latin in 1628, announcing that the blood circulates. Willis, a Scottish physician and scholar, gave English readers their standard version.

Harvey showed by experiment and by counting that the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make or use up. Valves in the veins, the ligature test on the arm, and the beating heart of cold-blooded animals all pointed one way. The blood must travel in a circle. The discovery remade physiology, and Willis's translation carried it to Victorian medicine in Harvey's own order of proof.
longfellow-evangeline-1847:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published Evangeline in 1847, and it made him the most beloved poet in America. Longfellow, a Harvard professor, heard the story of the Acadian exiles at a dinner party. He shaped it into an epic in English hexameters, a bold experiment for the time.

In 1755 the British expelled the French Acadians from Nova Scotia, scattering families across America. Evangeline Bellefontaine is parted from her betrothed, Gabriel, on their wedding day. She searches for him for years, through wilderness and new settlements, aging into a Sister of Mercy. The lovers meet at last in a Philadelphia hospital, too late. Generations of schoolchildren memorized the poem, and Acadia still keeps her shrine.
heine-atta-troll-1847:
Heinrich Heine wrote Atta Troll as a verse tale in the 1840s, and it appeared in 1847. Herman George Scheffauer translated the poem into English in 1913. Atta Troll is a dancing bear who escapes his keeper in the Pyrenees and dreams of bear freedom in the wild.

Heine uses the bear's story to mock the earnest political verse of his day. Hunters, witches, and the Wild Hunt cross the bear's path in wild scenes. The verse dances even while the satire bites. Heine called the poem a last free forest song of Romanticism. It stands as his great verse satire, funny on its face and sharp underneath, aimed at German complacency.
turgenev-jew-and-other-stories-1847:
Constance Garnett translated the early tales in The Jew and Other Stories from Ivan Turgenev's first years as a writer. The title story, written in the 1840s, is set amid the Napoleonic wars in Germany. A young Russian officer tells how an army spy, a Jewish sutler, was caught and hanged despite his pleas.

Other tales here try out themes Turgenev later mastered: first love, wasted lives, and kind hearts in hard places. The hand is younger and the plots lean on chance more than in his novels. Still, the clear prose and sympathy that mark his best work are present. The volume lets readers watch a major novelist learning his trade story by story.
andersen-improvisatore-howitt-1847:
Hans Christian Andersen published The Improvisatore in Denmark in 1835, and Mary Howitt Englished it in 1847. The novel made Andersen famous across Europe a decade before his fairy tales ruled nurseries. Antonio, a poor Roman boy with a gift for improvised song, tells his own story from childhood onward.

Antonio rises from street singer to admired performer, through love, loss, and patronage. Rome, Naples, and Venice glow in the background of his fortunes. Andersen drew on his own Italian travels and his hunger for recognition. Howitt, a tireless carrier of Scandinavian writing into English, gave the book its English life. It stands apart from the tales, as his great novel of the artist.
coverdale-bible-1535-bagster-1847:
Miles Coverdale gave England its first complete printed Bible in 1535, working from Latin and German versions where his Hebrew and Greek ran short. Samuel Bagster's 1847 reprint, the second modern edition, keeps the original text and spelling. The Apocrypha stands in its old place within the set.

Coverdale's phrasing of the Psalms proved so fine that the Church of England kept it in its prayer book for centuries. Lines like his rendering of the twenty-third Psalm still echo in English worship. The 1535 book was printed abroad and smuggled home at real risk. Bagster's reprint let Victorian readers hold the Tudor Bible as its first readers saw it.
william-malmesbury-chronicle-kings-engla:
William of Malmesbury wrote his Gesta Regum Anglorum, the Deeds of the Kings of England, in the 1120s, and it runs to the year 1127. J. A. Giles translated it into English in 1847. William is judged the greatest English historian of the twelfth century, a monk who read widely and weighed what he read.

From the Saxon kings to Henry I, he tells of courts, bishops, wars, and wonders with a fair and curious mind. He collected tales at first hand and marked what he doubted. His portraits of William the Conqueror and his sons still anchor the story of Norman England. Giles's version made the Latin monk a household name for English readers.
schwann-microscopical-researches-smith-1:
Theodor Schwann announced the cell theory in his Microscopical Researches, Englished by Henry Smith in 1847. The Sydenham Society published Smith's translation of the German work. Schwann argued that all living things, plant and animal alike, are built of cells. Structure and growth follow the same plan in both kingdoms.

He compares tissues under the microscope and traces how cells form and change. Eggs, embryos, and adult parts all fall under his single scheme. The book founded cell biology as a shared field. Its claim unified two sciences that had grown apart. Readers still cite it as a founding document. The evidence is patient and close.
boole-mathematical-analysis-logic-1847:
George Boole published The Mathematical Analysis of Logic as a pamphlet in 1847. In those few pages he founded symbolic logic. Boole treated reasoning as a calculus, with symbols that could be joined and split by rule. Deduction became something like algebra, open to exact handling.

He shows how class terms and statements turn into equations. From those equations, valid conclusions follow by fixed steps. The pamphlet's claims were bold for a self taught Irish mathematician. Later thinkers built Boolean algebra on this start. That algebra now runs inside every computer on Earth. The seed text is short enough to read in one sitting.
snow-ether-inhalation-1847:
John Snow turned to surgical anesthesia in his 1847 pamphlet on inhaling ether vapour. Ether had just entered surgery, and doses were guesswork. Snow made the first scientific study of how much vapour a patient needs. He built an inhaler to give a measured, steady dose.

Case reports from operations show the method at work on real patients. Snow records pulse, breathing, and depth of sleep with care. His aim was to make painless surgery safe as well as possible. The pamphlet marks the birth of anesthesia as a measured craft. Snow later became the queen's own chloroform doctor. The first edition holds the founding study.
zoist-vol-05-1847:
Volume five of The Zoist spans March 1847 to January 1848. Elliotson's journal carries mesmerism into its fifth year of print. Surgery under trance still fills reports, though ether now rivals the method. Cerebral physiology articles tie brain form to mental traits, as phrenology taught.

Somnambulist wonders and plain cures stand side by side in the record. Contributors argue over what the trance state truly is. The journal remains the English movement's chief archive, bound to reach thirteen volumes. Volume five shows a cause adapting to a changed world. Its case files preserve practice that journals of rank ignored. The primary detail is the value.
wood-choir-gaure-stonehenge-1747:
John Wood, the Bath architect, turned his eye to Stonehenge in 1747 and produced Choir Gaure. Wood measured the ring on Salisbury Plain and set down what he found in careful detail. He also offered his own bold reading of what the stones had been for.

Wood held that Druid priests built the ring as a temple tied to the moon. He tried to show how the stones might once have stood, in effect restoring the ruin on paper. His answer pushed back against William Stukeley, the best known Stonehenge writer of the age, and gave readers a rival, richly drawn account.
schoolcraft-notes-on-the-iroquois-1847:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft worked as an Indian agent in the Great Lakes region and married into an Ojibwe family, giving him rare access to native knowledge. His 1847 book gathers what he learned about the Iroquois confederacy, the powerful league of nations in New York.

Schoolcraft covers Iroquois government, the council system, and the condolence council that mourned dead chiefs and raised new ones. He retells myths and traditions and prints Iroquois pictographs, the picture records used to hold memory. Though later scholars corrected some of his claims, the book shaped American views of the Iroquois for generations.
demorgan-formal-logic-1847:
Augustus De Morgan, a London professor of math, published Formal Logic in 1847. Logic at the time still followed rules set by Aristotle two thousand years before. De Morgan set out to give the subject a sharper, more exact form.

He treats reasoning as a kind of calculus, where statements can be combined by clear rules. The book widens logic to cover relations and quantities, not just simple class terms. The pair of rules now called De Morgan's laws appears here in print. Later thinkers built modern symbolic logic on ground he cleared. It also picks sharp fights with the logic teaching of his day.
plos-pone-0003447:

An enzyme called PP2A removes a phosphate tag from p107. That removal proved critical for the cell cycle arrest FGF causes. Faulty FGF receptors cause several genetic skeletal disorders. Pinpointing this step names a place where the faulty signal might be softened.
plos-pone-0003547:
Robert Brudevold, Torstein Hole, and Jens Hammerstrøm studied high ferritin levels in patients in this 2008 paper. Referrals for hyperferritinemia had risen over ten years. Awareness of an iron overload disease and its gene test drove many referrals. Yet most referred patients had no iron overload at all.

In those patients, high ferritin linked to insulin resistance and fatty liver. Ferritin stores iron, but here it flagged metabolic trouble instead. The work reframes a common lab result as a warning sign. It may spare patients needless iron-focused testing. Fatty liver is rising fast with obesity in most rich countries.
plos-pone-0003647:
Carola Engler, Romy Kandzia, and Sylvestre Marillonnet published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cloning means joining DNA pieces in a set order to build new constructs. Older methods often leave extra sequence scars in the final product. The team set out to remove that flaw.

Their method joins pieces in one pot and one step, with precise joins and no leftover recombination sites. It also works at high throughput, so many constructs can be built at once. For labs, it offers a cleaner and faster route to assembled genes than the tools it replaced.
plos-pone-0003747:
Anan Yaghmur, Peter Laggner, Mats Almgren, and colleagues published this materials study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Monoelaidin is a fat-like compound that assembles itself in water into tiny structures. With a polymer stabilizer present, those structures change with temperature. The team watched the changes closely.

Using X-ray scattering and cryo-electron microscopy, they proved a direct shift from simple vesicles to cubosomes. Cubosomes are particles with a complex inner grid. Mapping this self-assembly guides designs for drug delivery particles built from such shape-shifting fats. Heat alone drove the change, with no new parts added.
plos-pone-0003847:
Gianni Panagiotou, Mikael R. Andersen, Thomas Grotkjær, and colleagues published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Aspergillus nidulans is a model fungus, close kin to species used in industry. The team identified the gene for a metabolic route in it called the phosphoketolase pathway.

Through systems analysis they unfolded how that pathway relates to the fungus's growth. The route reroutes sugar breakdown, and its activity sets part of the mold's pace of life. The work shows how a metabolic shortcut can shape growth in a model eukaryote used across cell biology.
plos-pone-0003947:
Klaus M. Stiefel, Boris S. Gutkin, and Terrence J. Sejnowski modeled how a brain chemical resets neuron timing in 2008. Cortical neurons fire spikes shaped by many inner currents. A phase response curve shows how a nudge shifts the next spike's timing. Neuromodulators can reshape that curve in living tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article studies acetylcholine, a classic modulator in the cortex. They report it changes both the shape and type of the response curve. That change alters how pyramid-shaped cortical neurons sync with inputs. The result helps explain how attention chemicals retune brain circuits.
plos-pone-0004047:

The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 10 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 347 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1861-d47:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. It is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The two men wrote past each other across the ocean, each unaware of the other's page. Adams reported his first dealings in London while Seward drafted stern orders at home. The matched date shows how wide the gap was between the post and the capital. The British proclamation of neutrality came that same week, which raised the stakes of each page.
frus-1861-d147:
William Dayton sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1861. It is document 147 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A second report in one day points to more than one live thread in Paris. Dayton split his points as Seward split his orders. The letter adds depth to a crowded week in the French file of 1861. Threads in Paris ranged from cotton prices to the fate of ships in French yards. Each thread he held was thin alone and strong only in the whole weave.
frus-1861-d247:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 15 August 1861. It stands as Document 247 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d47:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 14 April 1862. It stands as Document 47 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d147:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 19 September 1862, addressing Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The dispatch survives as Document 147 in the 1862 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's printed record of its dealings abroad.

Two days earlier the armies had met at Antietam, and President Lincoln was about to act on slavery. Word of both moves would reach Europe slowly and could shift how London saw the war. A short official letter like this one was the tool Washington had for guiding its envoy through fast-moving weeks. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d247:
A second Seward dispatch to Paris followed on 28 December 1861, printed as Document 247 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in three days mark the New Year rush of business after the Trent settlement. Dayton needed fresh guidance for a French government that was landing troops in Mexico that very month, alongside Britain and Spain. The pairing of these dispatches shows Washington trying to steady two fronts at once as 1862 began. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d347:
The Paris file in this run closes with a Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 21 November 1862, printed as Document 347 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Late November found the joint-action danger past for the year and France turning its energy back to Mexico. Seward's letter of this date belongs to the winding down of the autumn crisis in the Paris channel. It ends the Dayton sequence on the steadier ground the Union had sought since spring. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d447:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 August 1862. It is Document 447 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consular letters rarely made headlines, but they carried the facts of everyday foreign business: trade, shipping, stranded seamen, and citizens in trouble. Kreismann wrote from a capital friendly to the Union in a month when Union arms were stalled in Virginia. A consul's report also passed along the talk of the streets and papers, which ministers sometimes missed. The letter adds a ground-level Prussian view to the volume's record of the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d547:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 September 1862. His note is Document 547 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, with the heading punctuated as printed in the volume.

Van Limburg wrote a week after Lincoln's preliminary emancipation order, which changed the moral weather of every diplomatic conversation in Washington. The Dutch, strongly antislavery at home, received that change with interest. The formal business of the note belonged to the usual file of trade and neutral right, but it was transacted in a new atmosphere. The letter belongs to the early autumn Dutch papers. In them the reader can sense the war becoming a different kind of war. In European eyes, it was no longer the war of the spring.
frus-1862-d647:
Writing on 5 May 1862, Robert H. Pruyn sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Pruyn had just taken charge of the American legation in Japan, a post set up only in the late 1850s. The letter stands as document 647 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

In these first weeks Pruyn wrote home about the legation's work and his dealings with Japan's rulers. Such reports were how Washington learned what its envoys saw, weeks after the fact, since mail moved by ship. The dispatch is one link in the chain that kept a young trade link alive during a war an ocean away.
frus-1863p1-d47:
Christopher G. Memminger wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 24 October 1862. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 47 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The treasury's letters to London dealt with the South's thin purse: loans, cotton, and the bills that piled up in Europe. Memminger wrote to the man who faced the bankers and the British press. This letter is one of the money papers in the Confederate group printed here. It shows the war's other front, fought with credit in the counting houses of London.
frus-1863p1-d147:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 147 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

April mail from London followed up the seizure of the Southern raider and weighed what would come next in the yards. Adams kept his reports plain and full, as Seward liked them. This dispatch is a mid-run piece of that follow-up. It shows the legation turning a win into a watch: one ship held did not end the South's hopes in Britain, and Adams knew it.
frus-1863p1-d247:
Writing from London on 24 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 247 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d347:
The American answer to London on 31 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 347 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d447:
On 4 April 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d547:
On 1 June 1863 a formal note passed from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d647:
On 24 October 1863, William H. Seward, Secretary of State wrote to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020247:
Seth Blackshaw, Sanjiv Harpavat, Jeff Trimarchi, and a large team charted eye development in mice in PLOS Biology in 2004. The retina, the light-sensing sheet at the back of the eye, grows from a pool of stem-like cells. The team measured gene activity across that growth, stage by stage.

Their atlas shows which genes turn on as retinal cells split into the many types a working eye needs. Such a timeline is a base map for the whole field. It helps labs spot the genes behind inherited blindness and check whether stem cell work is on the right track. It also offers a model of how any complex tissue sorts itself out over time.
plos-pone-0000147:
Shixi Chen, Yu Wang, Fuyong Chen, and colleagues published this veterinary study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports that a highly pathogenic strain of the bacterium Staphylococcus sciuri caused fatal exudative epidermitis in piglets. That skin disease, known on farms for its greasy, crusting sores, can kill young pigs quickly.

S. sciuri is usually a mild organism found on animal skin, so a deadly strain stands out. The authors document the outbreak strain and its effects. The report warns pig producers and vets that a familiar bacterium can turn dangerous, and it adds to the record of emerging animal pathogens.
plos-pone-0000247:
Vincenzo D'Angiolella, Luca Palazzo, Concetta Santarpia, and colleagues published this cell cycle paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. M-phase promoting factor is the engine that drives a cell through mitosis, and it must be switched off for the cell to exit division. The authors report a role for non-proteolytic control, switching the engine off without destroying its parts.

Cells were known to exit mitosis by breaking down key proteins. A non-destructive off-switch adds another layer to that control. The finding refines the model of how division ends cleanly, a process whose failure can scramble chromosomes and feed cancer.
plos-pone-0000347:
Laurent Gillet, Heiko Adler, and Philip G. Stevenson published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Glycosaminoglycans are sugary chains on cell surfaces that many viruses grab as a first handhold. The authors study their interactions in infection by murine gammaherpesvirus-68, a mouse virus used to model human herpesviruses like Epstein-Barr.

A model virus lets researchers dissect infection steps that are hard to study in humans. The paper clarifies how much this virus depends on those surface sugars. The findings apply to the wider herpesvirus family, whose members infect most people for life.
plos-pone-0000447:
Laurent Jannière and colleagues presented genetic evidence connecting two core processes of the bacterial cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The processes are glycolysis, the breakdown of sugar for energy, and DNA replication, the copying of the genome before division. The link between them emerged from genetics rather than from chemistry alone.

That a sugar-burning pathway should talk to the genome-copying machinery is not obvious. Evidence of such a link suggests the cell coordinates its energy supply with its growth program instead of running each in isolation. Genetic evidence of this type often opens a field, inviting others to find the physical connection behind it.
plos-pone-0000547:
Diego Calzolari and colleagues took selective control of the cell's suicide network, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Apoptosis is the orderly self-destruction of a cell, run by a network of signaling proteins. Real cell populations are heterogeneous, a mix of types, and the team worked on selective control of the apoptosis signaling network in such mixed populations.

Selectivity is the crux of cancer therapy: trigger apoptosis in tumor cells while sparing the rest. A method that reads and steers the network cell by cell could find the exact lever for each type. The work is computational and systems-level, treating cell death as a controllable circuit.
plos-pone-0000647:
Fanny Mochel, Perrine Charles, François Seguin and colleagues searched blood for an early sign of Huntington disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is a fatal brain disorder with no effective treatment, and its root mechanisms remain unclear. Weight loss is a characteristic feature, appearing alongside chorea, the jerky movements, and cognitive decline.

The team reports an early energy deficit in patients and identifies a plasma biomarker that can be traced as disease progresses. A measurable blood sign matters when a disease is otherwise tracked by symptoms alone. It could help doctors follow progression and give future trials a way to tell whether a treatment changes the disease course.
plos-pone-0000747:
Luca Bolzoni, Leslie Real and Giulio De Leo modeled how uneven spread changes the control of new diseases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Controlling the emergence and spread of infections depends on many details at once. Pathogen and host genetics both matter, as do immunity, behavior, and ecology. So does the pattern of contacts over time and space among age and stage groups. Transmission heterogeneity means some cases infect many others while most infect few.

When spread is that lopsided, average-based strategies misfire. Targeting the settings and groups that drive transmission can beat blanket measures. Modelers built this study to compare control strategies under realistic unevenness, a question every emerging outbreak poses to health authorities.
plos-pone-0000847:
Gabriela Moura and colleagues compared codon pairs across many genomes, hunting the rules of the genetic code's usage, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Codon usage and codon-pair context are important features of gene structure that influence how faithfully messenger RNA is decoded into protein. To identify general rules shaping codon-pair context and minimizing decoding error, the team carried out a large-scale comparative analysis.

Their title says the analysis unveils general rules that fine-tune the evolution of mRNA primary structure. Genes are not written in any codon order that works; neighboring codon choices are tuned. Such rules matter for designing synthetic genes that cells need to read accurately.
plos-pone-0000947:
Stephen Beckstrom-Sternberg, Raymond Auerbach, Shubhada Godbole and colleagues fully characterized the genome of a dangerous tularemia strain, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, a disease that can kill and could be used as a weapon. The type A branch, found in North America, is the most severe form.

The team present a complete genomic characterization of a pathogenic A.II strain. A full genome lets scientists compare strains, trace outbreaks and spot what makes this branch so harmful. It also supports work on detection and vaccines. For a germ on watch lists, open reference data is a basic defense tool.
plos-pone-0001047:
Martin van Vliet, Christiaan Klijn, Lodewyk Wessels and colleagues predicted breast cancer outcomes using gene modules, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Labs had gathered large collections of tumor gene data, called compendia, yet outcome predictors rarely used them. Grouping genes into pathways, or modules, was also usually ignored in training.

The authors build prediction around modules instead of single genes. A compendium enlarges the training ground, and modules keep the model tied to biology rather than noise. Predicting which breast cancers turn dangerous guides treatment intensity. A method that uses public data better is a gain for every clinic that cannot gather its own.
plos-pone-0001147:
Early birth is a leading cause of death in newborns. About 40 percent of early births follow the premature rupture of the amnion, the membrane sac around the fetus. Che Connon and co-authors probed why that membrane breaks, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Rupture is thought to involve loss of collagen, the protein that gives the membrane strength.

Using X-ray diffraction, a method that reveals molecular structure, the authors studied the biomechanics of the amnion. Their work connects the membrane's collagen architecture to its breaking point. Understanding that structure is a step toward predicting or preventing dangerous early rupture.
plos-pone-0001247:
Light does more than let us see: it also sets alertness and cognition, through special cells in the retina that respond best to blue light. Gilles Vandewalle and colleagues compared brain responses to violet, blue, and green light in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. These nonvisual responses are thought to be mediated partly by melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells.

The authors report a prominent role for blue light and for the brainstem in these responses. Long retinal light exposure modulated brain activity even though the task was not visual. Their findings support the design of lighting that works with, not against, the brain's light sensors.
plos-pone-0001347:
Heart failure is usually studied one data type at a time. Anyela Camargo and Francisco Azuaje combined two: gene expression and functional network data, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Gene expression profiling and protein-protein interaction network analysis may together support the identification of disease biomarkers and potential drug targets.

The authors link the two data types for human heart failure, asking which network positions and expression changes coincide. That joint view is the point of their approach. A gene that both changes activity and sits at a network hub is a stronger candidate than either signal alone. Their study develops systems approaches to medicine.
plos-pone-0001447:
Yuan Wang and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eye growth in fruit flies. Cell surface sensors must be switched on to send growth signals, then switched off at the right time and place. A protein called Cbl helps with that shut off. The team studied its role as the fly eye forms.

They show the fly form of Cbl is vital for cell death and cell fate choices in the eye. When it fails, cells live or take fates they should not. The eye is a classic test bed for growth control. Findings there often map to broader rules for how tissues build themselves in the right pattern.
plos-pone-0001547:
R. Brad Jones and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV drugs and a human jumping gene. The jumping gene, LINE-1, is the sole one in our genome that can copy itself on its own. Its jumps in germ cells have caused gene ills. HIV drugs block a kin enzyme, so the team asked if they also block LINE-1.

They found the drugs do curb LINE-1 jumps, but to unlike degrees by drug. That split matters for both HIV care and gene safety. It hints these drugs could be reused where LINE-1 jumps drive harm. It also flags a side effect to watch in long term HIV care.
plos-pone-0001647:
Yanzhuang Wang, Jen-Hsuan Wei, Blaine Bisel, and their co-authors studied the Golgi body, the cell's shipping center, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In mammal cells the Golgi is made of flattened sacs packed into stacks. The team used a stacking protein called GRASP65 to change how tightly those sacs are packed.

They built a test to measure how fast proteins move through the Golgi to the cell surface. When the stacks were loosened, budding of small transport sacs, called COPI vesicles, sped up, and protein transport changed with it. The full text gives the assay, the imaging, and the transport rates. The results speak to a basic question: why the Golgi keeps its neat stacked shape, and what that shape does for the cell.
plos-pone-0001747:
Ruth M. Risueño, Wolfgang W. A. Schamel, and Balbino Alarcón studied how the T cell receptor changes shape when it engages a target, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The receptor must tell apart closely related peptide-MHC ligands and turn that judgment into different signals. One model holds that strong ligands force a shape change in the receptor.

The team reports that on engagement, the receptor's CD3ε and CD3ζ subunits adopt a compact, locked conformation. The full text gives the shape measurements and which ligands trigger the lock. A physical lock-and-key step inside the cell would explain how T cells convert tiny differences outside into firm decisions, a core puzzle of immunity.
plos-pone-0001847:
Peter McErlean, Laura A. Shackelton, Emily Andrews, and their co-authors described a putative new rhinovirus species in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human rhinoviruses cause most acute respiratory tract infections that labs detect. Yet little was known about how common each kind is, how often it returns, its structure, and its clinical impact. In 2007 the full gene codes of six unknown rhinoviruses became available.

The team sets out the molecular traits and clinical features of the proposed new species, human rhinovirus C. The full text gives the sequence contrasts and patient data. A whole missed species of the common cold virus changes respiratory tracking and may explain infections that older tests read as negative.
plos-pone-0001947:
Chetana Sachidanandan and co-authors found a new growth signal by screening small molecules in fish embryos, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Small molecules have long helped map the paths that build an embryo and drive disease. The search for fresh ones that tune those paths has driven large screens of chemical libraries.

The team screened compounds in zebrafish embryos, whose clear bodies let shifts in growth be seen at a glance. They report the find of a novel retinoid, a kin of vitamin A signals that shape the body plan. A new signal of this class gives labs a fresh tool to probe growth.
plos-pone-0002047:
Aymone Gurtner and co-authors studied gene tags that split dividing cells from resting ones, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Switching genes on or off calls for chemical changes to histones, the spools DNA winds on, which reshape chromatin, the packed form of DNA. How that structure is tuned as cells stop dividing was under intense study.

The team focused on NF-Y, a protein that binds a common gene switch motif. They report that epigenetic marks set with NF-Y's help discriminate between proliferating tissue and postmitotic tissue, where cells have left the cycle for good. Such marks may lock in the resting state.
plos-pone-0002147:
Sigrun Roeber, Eva-Maria Grasbon-Frodl, Otto Windl, and co-authors reported new gene changes tied to a rare brain disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease destroys the brain, and the inherited form can look just like cases that arise with no family history. Finding fresh mutations in the prion protein gene, PRNP, is thus a key part of telling the forms apart.

The team found two different rare changes at one spot in the gene, codon 188. They present the clinical and tissue evidence that these changes play a part in causing the disease. Each confirmed mutation sharpens testing for families at risk.
plos-pone-0002247:
Roy Varshavsky, David Horn, and Michal Linial looked for global patterns in how data are clustered, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hierarchy, with tree-like branching, is a natural way to organize data in many fields. The standard tool is bottom-up hierarchical clustering, which merges the closest items step by step until one tree remains.

The authors used global considerations, looking at the whole tree at once rather than single merges, to reveal patterns that local methods miss. Their approach can show meaningful groupings in data sets from biology and beyond. Better clustering matters wherever scientists sort thousands of items, from genes to documents, into families.
plos-pone-0002347:
Tsin Yeo, Daniel Lampah, Retno Gitawati, and co-authors checked the safety of an amino acid infusion in malaria patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. L-arginine improves endothelial function, the health of blood vessel linings, which malaria damages. Its safety profile in this disease, though, had not been described in detail.

The team assessed symptoms, blood pressure and circulation, and blood chemistry before and after a single L-arginine infusion in adults with moderately severe falciparum malaria. A careful safety record is the gate any add-on treatment must pass. Their report gives clinicians the baseline needed before larger trials test whether the infusion also helps patients recover.
plos-pone-0002447:
West and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jason B. West, Adam Sobek, James R. Ehleringer, among others. Its subject is a Simplified GIS Approach to Modeling Global Leaf Water Isoscapes. The hydrogen and oxygen isotope ratios of materials record biological and physical processes as reactions proceed.

The paper uses those ratios to model global leaf water isoscapes, which are maps of isotope patterns in leaf water. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002547:
Cornuz joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Jacques Cornuz, Susanne Zwahlen, Walter Felix Jungi, among others. Its subject is a Vaccine against Nicotine for Smoking Cessation: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Tobacco dependence is the leading cause of preventable death and disabilities worldwide and nicotine is the main substance responsible for the addiction to tobacco.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002647:
A 2008 study by László Zsolt Garamszegi and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up birds reveal their personality when singing. The catalog record names László Zsolt Garamszegi first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Individual differences in social behaviour may have consequences for mate choice and sexual signalling. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002747:
Djin-Ye Oh and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was CCR5Δ32 genotypes in a german HIV-1 seroconverter cohort and report of HIV-1 infection in a CCR5Δ32 homozygous individual. Authorship is credited in the record to Djin-Ye Oh and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Homozygosity (Δ32/Δ32) for the 32 bp deletion in the chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) gene is associated with strong resistance against HIV infection. It goes on to note a further point. Heterozygosity is associated with protection of HIV-1 disease progression. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002847:
Haixi Miao and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was gene expression and functional studies of the optic nerve head astrocyte transcriptome from normal african americans and caucasian americans donors. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Haixi Miao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. To determine whether optic nerve head (ONH) astrocytes, a key cellular component of glaucomatous neuropathy. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002947:
Nancy Cladel, Jiafen Hu, Karla Balogh and co-authors recoded a papillomavirus gene in 2008 to see what changed. Papillomaviruses use rare codons, the three-letter DNA words for amino acids, compared with their hosts. Matching viral codons to host ones can raise protein output, past studies had shown.

The team optimized codons in the CRPV E7 gene without changing the protein itself. Growth and immunity shifted, including after E7 vaccination. Published in PLOS ONE, the result warns vaccine designers that silent DNA changes are not always silent in the body. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003047:
Sandra Taylor and Katherine Pollard compared two methods for estimating bird populations in 2008. Effective management depends on tracking how bird numbers trend over time, and sometimes on estimating total abundance. Two methods had been advocated for such studies: double observer and double sampling.

Published in PLOS ONE, the evaluation sets the two against each other so field crews can choose with evidence. Double observer uses paired counters; double sampling pairs quick counts with intensive ones. Getting trends right matters because management money follows the numbers these methods produce. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003147:
Sera L. Young, M. Jeffrey Wilson, Dennis Miller and colleagues tackle a methods gap on pica in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Pica is the craving for and eating of non-food items such as earth, charcoal and raw starch. It has puzzled people for more than two thousand years, yet few data exist to test the main ideas about it, in part due to weak methods.

The authors propose a full approach to collecting and analysing pica substances, with a focus on earth-eating materials. Readers get practical steps for field and lab work on a neglected behaviour. Better samples should let future studies test why pica occurs and whether it harms or helps.
plos-pone-0003247:
Genc Basha, Gregory Lizée, Anna T. Reinicke and colleagues trace antigen handling in dendritic cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cross-presentation by dendritic cells is a crucial prerequisite for effective priming of cytotoxic T-cell responses against bacterial, viral and tumour antigens. However, this antigen presentation pathway remains poorly defined. The team set out to develop a comprehensive understanding of it.

They report that MHC class I endosomal and lysosomal trafficking coincides with exogenous antigen loading in dendritic cells. Readers follow the route foreign material takes to reach the display system. That route is a target for improving vaccines that need strong T-cell responses.
plos-pone-0003347:
Hilda Fragoso-Loyo and co-authors test antibody measures in lupus that affects the brain in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. arxiv-2606-16047: When people argue, some claims support others and some attack them — mapping those relations is key to understanding debates. This paper sets up a multi-agent debate system where AI agents argue about argument structure, with "confidence gating" deciding which relations to trust. It converts the components of an argument into a graph of support and attack links.
arxiv-2606-15847: Floer math is a prized engine for counting loop paths in twisty shape-space. This paper lays the base stones of a whole-number take on it — sums over 1, 2, 3… not smooth reals — which nets finer catch. Base-laying math for shape-space pros.
arxiv-2606-16247: Databases pick the order in which to join tables, and a bad order makes queries crawl. This paper improves join-order optimization using hybrid quantum-classical methods for QUBO problems — a mathematical form quantum hardware handles well. It targets database and quantum-computing researchers exploring practical quantum speedups.
arxiv-2606-16547: The 'dark bubble' yarn says our all sits in a blown bubble in a wider deep. This paper weighs light waves that tug themselves — light held by its own heft — inside that yarn. Far-out sky yarn for all-shape dreamers.
arxiv-2606-16647: Line-up math (normal order) files quirk bits in neat rows — a shop-worn aid. This paper widens the old Bell count-rows that bloom from wide line-ups, and charts the new rows' kin laws. For count-row sages and quirk-math fans. Wide rows, wide reach.
arxiv-2606-16847: Diffusion language models write by unmasking text step by step — but they can wander. This paper steers them with a 'latent roadmap': anchor tokens that mark the route, allowing revocable decoding (backing up when wrong). It is for researchers improving diffusion-based text generation.
